short: Britain's first prime minister in all but name, and its longest-serving.
full:
Robert Walpole took charge of the Treasury in April 1721 amid the wreckage of the South Sea Bubble, a speculative collapse that had ruined thousands and discredited much of the political class. He was never formally called prime minister - the phrase began as an insult from his opponents - but his grip on the Commons, the Treasury and royal patronage under George I and George II created the office in practice.

He held power for almost twenty-one years, longer than anyone since. His method was peace abroad, a low land tax at home, and the systematic distribution of places and pensions to secure Commons majorities. He kept Britain out of European wars until public agitation forced the War of Jenkins' Ear in 1739, and that war's mismanagement finished him: he resigned in February 1742 and took an earldom. 10 Downing Street, given to him by George II, has housed his successors ever since.
